unit: Romeo and Juliet by William Shakespeare

findings.claim: Romeo ... poisons himself beside Juliet’s body just as she wakes.
findings.truth: Romeo takes poison and dies before Juliet wakes.
findings.evidence: Folger Shakespeare, Act 5 Scene 3

findings.claim: Extended set-text answers should combine design and performer choices, including a playwright’s-intentions question.
findings.truth: The 20-mark set-text task is answered as either a performer or a designer; it is not a combined directorial or playwright-intentions task.
findings.evidence: spec 4.2; AQA Bringing assessment to life, GCSE Section B

findings.claim: The Nurse has almost all her dialogue in prose, with Act Four as the exception when she shifts into verse.
findings.truth: The Nurse uses both prose and verse, including verse before Act Four.
findings.evidence: Folger Shakespeare, Acts 1.3 and 4.5

findings.claim: The chorus figure ... does not return until the epilogue.
findings.truth: The Chorus appears for the Act One and Act Two prologues; there is no Chorus epilogue.
findings.evidence: Folger Shakespeare, Prologue and Act 2 Chorus

findings.claim: The 12-mark set-text task asks students to analyse the playwright’s intentions about themes.
findings.truth: The 12-mark set-text task is a performer task on use of performance space and interaction in the shaded extract.
findings.evidence: spec 4.2; AQA Bringing assessment to life, GCSE Section B

findings.claim: Context is assessed through playwright’s-intentions extended responses.
findings.truth: The context-linked set-text task is the 4-mark design question.
findings.evidence: spec 4.2; AQA Bringing assessment to life, GCSE Section B

findings.claim: A sonnet is typically an octave and sestet with a concluding rhyming couplet.
findings.truth: A Shakespearean sonnet has three quatrains and a concluding rhyming couplet.
findings.evidence: Folger, Reading Shakespeare’s Language: Sonnets; RSC Shakespeare Learning Zone, Romeo and Juliet first meeting

findings.claim: The Nurse, servants and Peter speak almost entirely in prose; in Act Four the Nurse shifts into verse.
findings.truth: The Nurse uses both prose and verse; the discovery-scene verse is not her sole departure from prose.
findings.evidence: Folger Shakespeare, Acts 1.3 and 4.5

findings.claim: The 12-mark task is an analyse-the-playwright’s-intentions question, while the 20-mark response combines performer and design work.
findings.truth: The 12-mark task is performer-focused; the 20-mark task is answered as either performer or designer.
findings.evidence: spec 4.2; AQA Bringing assessment to life, GCSE Section B

findings.claim: The Capulets are the family with social power in Verona.
findings.truth: The Prologue describes the two households as alike in dignity; the text does not establish a higher Capulet social rank.
findings.evidence: Folger Shakespeare, Prologue

findings.claim: Frantic Assembly created a physical-theatre Romeo and Juliet in 2008.
findings.truth: Frantic Assembly’s 2008 Shakespeare production was Othello.
findings.evidence: Frantic Assembly, Othello production page

findings.claim: The 8-mark set-text question is a designer question and the 20-mark response must cover all four design departments.
findings.truth: The 8-mark task is performer-focused; the 20-mark task is either a performer response or a response in one design skill.
findings.evidence: spec 4.2; AQA Bringing assessment to life, GCSE Section B

findings.claim: For the 20-mark question, bring in a designer’s perspective too.
findings.truth: The 20-mark set-text task requires either the performer role or one design skill, not both.
findings.evidence: spec 4.2; AQA Bringing assessment to life, GCSE Section B

findings.claim: Gestus is Brecht’s term for critical distance, also called the alienation effect.
findings.truth: Gestus is a clear physical expression of a social attitude or relationship; critical distance is the alienation effect.
findings.evidence: European Theatre Lexicon, Epic theatre

findings.claim: The 2008 Frantic Assembly production of Romeo and Juliet is the example of physical theatre for this play.
findings.truth: Frantic Assembly produced Othello in 2008, not Romeo and Juliet.
findings.evidence: Frantic Assembly, Othello production page

findings.claim: The question is always what a director drawing on a practitioner would do; a 20-mark response must compare approaches.
findings.truth: AQA’s set-text sequence has no distinct practitioner question. Its 20-mark task is a performer or single-design-skill response.
findings.evidence: spec 4.2; AQA Bringing assessment to life, GCSE Section B

findings.claim: The examiners’ most frequently noted error ... is treating Juliet as an older woman or generalising her age.
findings.truth: No examiner-feedback source establishing this claimed frequency was provided or fetched; retain only if a source is supplied.
findings.evidence: AQA specification and fetched assessment guidance give no ranked list of errors

findings.claim: Examiners consistently reward answers that hold multiple themes simultaneously.
findings.truth: This asserted pattern of examiner feedback was not sourced and could not be verified from the specification or assessment guidance.
findings.evidence: AQA specification; AQA Bringing assessment to life

findings.claim: Examiner feedback consistently identifies the same gap in performer answers.
findings.truth: No fetched examiner-feedback source substantiated this claimed consistency.
findings.evidence: AQA specification and fetched assessment guidance

findings.claim: For the original performances of Romeo and Juliet, Juliet was played by a boy actor.
findings.truth: Female roles in Shakespeare’s theatre were generally played by boys or young men, but no source fetched identifies the original Juliet actor. Either qualify this as likely or source the original cast record.
findings.evidence: Folger, Shakespeare’s Theater; no original Romeo and Juliet cast record found

findings.claim: Fathers had legal authority over daughters, and Capulet arranging Juliet’s marriage without asking was unremarkable to an original audience.
findings.truth: The paragraph conflates early modern social pressure, legal consent and the play’s own portrayal. The text first has Lady Capulet ask Juliet’s disposition, while historical authority and consequences varied. Revise with a sourced, qualified account rather than an absolute claim.
findings.evidence: Folger, Act 1 Scene 3; historical sources on early modern marriage and consent give a more qualified picture
findings.ruling: One hedging sentence appended; Lady Capulet's question noted.

summary: Checked all eight lessons against the specification, official AQA assessment guidance and fetched primary-text or theatre-company sources. Sixteen verified findings have surgical edits; two contextual-history claims need sourced qualification and three examiner-feedback claims remain unsupported notes.
